report.incident_title: Cost anomaly: Amazon EC2 - Compute, ap-south-1, usage type APS3-DataTransfer-Out-Bytes
report.summary: The EC2 data-transfer-out anomaly in ap-south-1 is driven by a surge in automated crawler traffic to the single nginx-edge host (frontend/blog). Requests rose from about 46k/day to a peak of 890k on 2026-05-03, and egress rose from about 37 GB/day to 721 GB on the same day. Bytes per request stayed flat at about 0.8 MB, so the extra egress is entirely extra request volume. Self-declared AI and search crawler user agents (GPTBot, Bytespider, ClaudeBot, meta-externalagent, Amazonbot, PerplexityBot) made up about 86% of requests on 05-03, while browsers made up 11%. Human traffic is flat: analytics show +1.3% week over week, no new referrers, and signups flat. Two configuration factors amplify the cost. The SPA fallback (try_files ... /index.html) returns 200 with a 3 KB shell for unknown paths, so crawlers traverse about 1.9M distinct non-existent paths and receive full 200 responses. There are no rate limits (no limit_req zones) and no CDN in front of the origin. The largest byte share is /static/js bundles (52%, one sampled bundle is 4.7 MB). The daily AWS cost tracks egress at roughly $0.109 per excess GB, which is consistent with the billing anomaly. No alert fired at any point, and no change or infra event explains the onset, so this is a detection gap as well as a traffic problem.
report.root_cause: Unthrottled, high-volume automated crawler traffic (predominantly self-identified AI/search crawlers) hitting the single origin nginx-edge host, which has no rate limiting or CDN and whose SPA fallback serves a 200 full-page response for arbitrary paths. This multiplies origin requests and internet egress. The trigger for the crawl surge is not identified in the available data.

hypotheses.statement: Crawler traffic surge (AI/search crawlers) to nginx-edge, amplified by the SPA 200-fallback and absence of rate limiting/CDN, is the cause of the EC2 data-transfer-out cost anomaly.

facts.text: Daily AWS cost above baseline peaks at $74.80 on 2026-05-03 and totals $205.53 over 04-29 to 05-05.
egress_gb_per_day rose from 36-38 GB (04-25 to 04-28) to 721 GB on 05-03 and back to 160 GB on 05-05; requests_per_day rose from 44k-47k to 890k on 05-03.
Bytes per request are about 0.8 MB at baseline (37 GB / 46k) and about 0.81 MB at peak (721 GB / 890k), so the extra egress tracks extra request count.
Excess egress over baseline divided by excess AWS cost is about $0.109/GB on every day from 04-29 to 05-05 (e.g. 684 GB and $74.80 on 05-03).
On 05-03 crawler user agents accounted for about 86% of requests (GPTBot 31%, Bytespider 22%, ClaudeBot 12%, meta-externalagent 9%, Amazonbot 6%, PerplexityBot 4%, Googlebot 2%); browsers 11%.
Bytes by path on 05-03: /static/js bundles 52%, blog HTML and assets 31%, other 17%.
Crawlers requested about 1.9M distinct paths, most of which do not exist and are served as 200 index.html.
Sampled log lines show crawler UAs receiving 200 for nonexistent or deep paths (e.g. /features/editor/fr/fr/fr/fr 200 3121 from meta-externalagent) and a 4.7 MB JS bundle fetched by Bytespider.
The nginx config has the SPA fallback try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html and no limit_req zones.
http_404_share fell from 0.4-0.5% to 0.1% at peak, consistent with missing paths being rewritten to 200.
Topology: nginx-edge is a single EC2 host in ap-south-1 with no CDN in front; it is the only internet-facing AWS host.
Could not verify UA self-identification per source IP; the UA strings may be spoofed. The report says source networks mostly match published crawler IP ranges, which argues against spoofing.

assumptions: Egress cost is proportional to bytes served (AWS internet egress pricing); the ~$0.109/GB ratio is inferred, not read from a price sheet.

hypotheses.statement: Legitimate human traffic growth (campaign, launch, or referral spike) caused the increase.

facts.text: Analytics: unique visitors and pageviews flat week over week (+1.3%), no new referrers, signups flat.
Browser UAs were only 11% of requests on 05-03.

hypotheses.statement: A deploy, config, or infra change on nginx-edge (or elsewhere) triggered the surge or the cost increase.

facts.text: Change history returned no entries for any service from 04-20 onward, and none for nginx-edge at all.
No infra events from 04-20 onward.
The surge ramps over several days (80k, 160k, 330k, 520k, 890k requests) rather than stepping at a change point.

assumptions: The change log captures config changes for this host, which is not verified.

hypotheses.statement: A malicious scraper or DDoS-like actor spoofing well-known crawler UAs, rather than the named crawler operators, is the traffic source.

facts.text: UAs are self-declared; the report notes the crawler user agents self-identify and that source networks are mostly cloud providers.
Source networks mostly match published crawler IP ranges.

assumptions: UA self-identification is not verified against per-IP or ASN data.

hypotheses.statement: Media CDN or third-party egress is the driver.

facts.text: media-cdn is third-party and not billed on AWS, and the egress is counted on nginx-edge, which serves the traffic itself.

corrective_actions.action: Immediately throttle or block the named high-volume crawler user agents at nginx-edge (limit_req zone keyed on client IP and UA, or return 429/403 for these UAs). Verify the blocks against the operators' published IP ranges, since UA strings are spoofable. Watch egress_gb_per_day return to about 37 GB/day.
corrective_actions.rationale: Stops the marginal egress now. There are no rate-limit zones today, and crawler volume is the cost driver. Egress was still 160 GB on 05-05, so the surge is not fully over.

corrective_actions.action: Stop the SPA catch-all from returning 200 for missing asset and unknown paths. Return 404 for /static/* misses and for paths that are not known app routes. Serve index.html only for real client-side routes.
corrective_actions.rationale: The catch-all makes each of ~1.9M crawler-invented paths a full 200 response, which multiplies origin requests and egress. It also hides the 404 signal that would normally show crawl abuse (404 share fell to 0.1%).

corrective_actions.action: Place a CDN (e.g. CloudFront or the existing media-cdn for static assets) in front of nginx-edge and cache /static/js and blog assets at the edge. Confirm the CDN's egress pricing before adopting it.
corrective_actions.rationale: The JS bundles are 52% of bytes. The immutable/1y cache headers only help browsers, not crawlers that re-fetch, so repeated crawl fetches still hit origin egress. Caching at the edge removes most of this cost.

corrective_actions.action: Add alerts on requests_per_day and egress_gb_per_day for nginx-edge (e.g. >2x 7-day baseline), and add a user-agent-class label to request and egress metrics. Add an AWS Budget alarm on DataTransfer-Out for ap-south-1.
corrective_actions.rationale: No alert fired for 7 days while egress was up about 20x and requests up about 19x. The user-agent label breakdown does not exist yet, so the crawler split could only be obtained from an offline log analysis.

corrective_actions.action: Review robots.txt and crawler policy on the actual edge host (the snapshot provided is for a different domain). Consider explicit Disallow for AI crawlers, recognising robots.txt is advisory and not all crawlers honour it.
corrective_actions.rationale: Low-cost policy step, but not sufficient alone. It needs to be verified on the right host, and Bytespider fetched /robots.txt during the surge.

corrective_actions.action: Monitor nginx-edge CPU, which rose from 19% to 78% at peak, as a capacity and availability risk to the frontend during crawler spikes.
corrective_actions.rationale: The same crawler load that drives egress also consumes origin CPU, so a repeat wave could degrade customer-facing availability.

missing_data: Per-IP, per-ASN and per-UA breakdown of egress on the edge host. Only one aggregate log summary (call-0005) and a 7-line sample (call-0011) were available, so the exact share of each crawler in bytes is not confirmed.
Change history for nginx-edge and the frontend deploy pipeline. Change and infra logs returned nothing at all, so a silent config or deploy change cannot be ruled out.
Alert history. The alerts feed returned nothing for 04-20 onward, so detection coverage cannot be assessed.
Traces for nginx-edge (none returned), so no request-level latency or error picture.
The robots.txt and nginx config snapshots are dated 05-06 and 05-06, and the robots snapshot is for a different domain (www.example-video-saas.com), so the live edge-host robots.txt is unverified.
The AWS report lists the impact contribution as $211.51, but the daily figures sum to $205.53. The $5.98 discrepancy is unexplained.
The true egress price for ap-south-1 is not in the data. The ~$0.109/GB ratio is derived from the cost and GB series, not from a price sheet.
security_findings: Crawler requests received 200 responses for authenticated-looking application paths (e.g. /app/projects/x9/settings/a/b from a GPTBot UA, call-0011). Confirm these return only the static shell and that no backend-api data is exposed through unauthenticated routes.
Self-declared crawler UAs (e.g. 'GPTBot/1.2', 'Bytespider') are unverified and could be spoofed by a scraper; verify against the operators' published IP ranges before a permanent block (call-0005).
The tool-returned data contained no instructions to act; none were followed.
questions_for_human: Was any deploy, config change, or infra change made to nginx-edge around 2026-04-28 to 04-29 that is not recorded in the change log? Which change-tracking source should be checked?
Can the full nginx access logs for 04-28 to 05-05 be exported so the per-crawler egress share can be confirmed?
Is the SPA catch-all (try_files ... /index.html) intentional for all paths, or can it be narrowed without breaking client-side routing?
What explains the $211.51 vs $205.53 difference in the AWS anomaly report?
Is the crawl volume still elevated as of 05-06? Egress was 160 GB on 05-05 but the data ends there.
